journeys.title: Find your way around
journeys.goal: See what the GUI is made of before changing anything in it.

steps.narrative: The sidebar on the left lists your notebooks. Help is one of them: the documentation is seeded into your library as ordinary read-only notes, so you can search it alongside everything else.

postcondition.narrative: the Help notebook is present in the sidebar

journeys.title: Write a note, and read it back
journeys.goal: Create a note and get something into it.

steps.narrative: Click New note. The note is created immediately and opens for editing; there is no dialog to fill in first.
Type into the editor. What you write is Markdown, and the preview beside it renders as you go.

postcondition.narrative: the editor is open with the note in it

journeys.title: Choose which notebook a note goes in
journeys.goal: File a note somewhere other than where it landed.

steps.narrative: Start from a new note.
Open the notebook picker. It sits with the note rather than in a menu, because which notebook a note belongs to is part of the note.

postcondition.narrative: the notebook picker is open and offering somewhere to file the note

journeys.title: Tag a note
journeys.goal: Put a tag on the note you are writing, and take one off.

steps.narrative: Start from a note. Tags belong to a note, so there has to be one open.

Open the tag control. It sits in the editor toolbar beside the notebook control, because both answer where this note belongs and both belong where you are typing. The label shows how many tags the note carries.
Type the tag. Tags are hierarchical, so `field/dusk` sits under `field`. Press Enter or use Add.
Add it. Each tag then appears as a chip with its own remove button, rather than as a comma-separated line you have to edit carefully.

postcondition.narrative: the tag control is showing the note's tags

journeys.title: Link one note to another
journeys.goal: Put a link to another note into the one you are writing, without leaving it to find the address.

steps.narrative: Open the note you want to link from. Everything that follows is in this note; the one you link to is never opened.

Note info holds what the note is rather than what it says: where it came from, what it links to, what is attached to it, and the tools for changing those. It is closed by default because a note you are reading is usually a note you are reading.
Type part of the other note’s title. The suggestions come from a search over titles, so you do not need the identifier and you do not need the note open in another window.
Choosing a suggestion writes a stable `document://` link into the body at the cursor. It is stable in the sense that matters: it names the note, so renaming the note later does not break it.
The link is in the body and the note is unsaved — the badge above the editor says so. Nothing was written for you: move the link to where it belongs in your prose first, then save.

postcondition.narrative: the note carries an unsaved change, which is the link that was just inserted

journeys.title: Change a note you already wrote
journeys.goal: Open an existing note, change it, and save the change.

steps.narrative: All notes is every note in the library, whichever notebook it is filed in. Start here when you know what a note is called but not where you put it.
Click a note in the results list to open it. The editor fills with the note as it stands; nothing is changed by opening it.
The title is an ordinary field at the top of the editor. Change it the way you would change any text.
Saving writes a new revision rather than overwriting the old one, so the version you just replaced is still there.

postcondition.narrative: the note is open with its new title, saved as a fresh revision

journeys.title: Delete a note
journeys.goal: Move a note to the Trash and confirm it arrived there.

steps.narrative: Find the note first. Deleting is something you do to an open note, not to a row in a list, so that it is always clear which note is about to go.
Open the note you mean to delete and read it once. This is the last screen on which its text is in front of you.

Deleting asks you to confirm, and names the note it is about to move so that a mis-clicked row cannot become a deleted note. Deleting moves it to the Trash; it is not destroyed, and nothing here empties the Trash on a timer.
Trash is a place you can open and look inside, not a countdown. The note is in it.

postcondition.narrative: the deleted note is listed in the Trash

journeys.title: Take a note back out of the Trash
journeys.goal: Restore a deleted note and confirm it is back among your notes.

steps.narrative: Open the Trash to see what is in it. Everything here was deleted and none of it is gone.
Open the note you want back. A trashed note opens read-only, with a badge saying why.
Restoring returns the note to the notebook it was filed in, not to some general inbox.
All notes again, to see it where it belongs.

postcondition.narrative: the restored note is listed among the notes again

journeys.title: Search for a note
journeys.goal: Find notes by what they say, using the same query language the command line takes.

steps.narrative: The search box takes the query language, not just a word. Bare words are combined with an implicit AND; an uppercase OR widens the search instead.
Run the search. Results are ordered by relevance and page as you scroll, so a large library does not have to be loaded to be searched.

postcondition.narrative: notes matching either side of the OR are listed

journeys.title: Narrow a search by tag, and exclude what you do not want
journeys.goal: Use a field query and a negation together, which is what most real searches turn out to be.

steps.narrative: tag: matches a tag rather than the note's text, and a leading minus excludes. Here that is everything tagged field/dusk except the documentation.
The same box runs it. Every query-language feature works here exactly as it does in notriosctl search, because it is the same parser.

postcondition.narrative: only the tagged note outside the Help notebook is listed

journeys.title: Keep a search as a notebook
journeys.goal: Turn a search you have just watched work into a notebook in the sidebar.

steps.narrative: Search for whatever you want the notebook to hold. Any query works: this is the same language the rest of the interface takes.
Run it and read the results. This is the point of keeping a search here rather than typing one into a form: you are deciding about a query you have watched work, not one you hope is right.
Keep this search appears once a search has returned something. A query that found nothing is not offered, because a notebook made from it would open empty.
The query is suggested as the name and is usually not what you want to read in a sidebar. The query itself is shown below the field but cannot be edited here.
Keeping it adds a notebook to the sidebar whose contents are whatever the query matches, now and later.

postcondition.narrative: the kept search is listed in the sidebar as a notebook

journeys.title: Rename a tag, and everything under it
journeys.goal: Change a tag's name across every note that carries it, after seeing what that will do.

steps.narrative: Tags are listed in the sidebar with the number of notes carrying each one. The pencil beside a tag renames it; the name itself still runs a search for it.
A rename reaches every note carrying the tag. Leaving “rename everything under it” ticked also moves the tags nested below this one.

Nothing has changed yet. The report is not a guess: the service performs the rename inside a transaction and rolls it back, so what you are reading and what applying would do cannot disagree. A change described as a merge means the destination already exists and the two tags become one.
Rename applies exactly what the report described. Editing the name or the children option first withdraws the report, so you cannot agree to one rename and apply another.

postcondition.narrative: the renamed tag is listed in the sidebar under its new name

journeys.title: Check what has rotted, and repair what can be
journeys.goal: See the library's problems, repair the mechanical ones, and know why the rest are commands.

steps.narrative: Health reads two reports about this library. Nothing on the screen changes anything: both reports are read-only, and one of them says so in the API itself.

Lint finds broken links, unresolved anchors, notes without titles, remote media nobody has localized, attachments nothing points at. Counts are for the whole library; where a list is capped it says so, because a capped list read as the whole problem undercounts it.

The collector plans, and never deletes. Deleting is notriosctl gc --apply, and the absence of a button here is deliberate: reclaiming space should be an explicit local act rather than something a window does.

Some findings can be corrected without judgement. Planning shows how many edits across how many notes and changes nothing; repairing applies them, each against the revision it was computed from, so a note you edited in the meantime refuses rather than being repaired against text nobody read. Collecting unreferenced attachments is not offered here: it deletes, and a repair only writes a new revision.

postcondition.narrative: both reports are on screen and nothing has been changed

journeys.title: Import a Joplin export
journeys.goal: Bring a Joplin RAW export into this library from the desktop app.

steps.narrative: Open **File ▸ Import and export…**, or press Ctrl+I. Everything that reads or writes a folder on this machine is here, and it is here only in the desktop app: a browser cannot open a folder, so these controls are shown there and disabled with that reason rather than hidden.

locator.native: the File menu's “Import and export…” item

expect: the import and export dialog opened

steps.narrative: Name the Joplin RAW export folder — the one Joplin wrote, with a Markdown file per note. **Choose folder…** opens a directory chooser if you would rather point at it. Nothing below is available until a folder is named.

Press **Import**, and the report says what arrived. **Scan without importing** sits beside it and writes nothing, which is the safer first move on an export you have not opened. Imported notes are ordinary editable notes: a migration, not a read-only attachment.

locator.native: the “Import” button in the Joplin section

postcondition.narrative: the imported notes are in the library

journeys.title: Export the whole library
journeys.goal: Write a portable archive of everything, from the desktop app.

steps.narrative: Open **File ▸ Import and export…**, or press Ctrl+I. Everything that reads or writes a folder on this machine is here, and it is here only in the desktop app: a browser cannot open a folder, so these controls are shown there and disabled with that reason rather than hidden.

locator.native: the File menu's “Import and export…” item

expect: the import and export dialog opened

steps.narrative: Name the folder to write the archive into, and let it be an empty one: an archive is a directory of files rather than a single file.

locator.native: the “Folder to write the archive into” field

steps.keys: Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab

steps.narrative: Press **Export everything**, and the report names what was written. Exporting a subset — by notebook, tag or query — stays on the command line, because choosing a subset means seeing what it selects before it is written. The same dialog reads an archive back: **Import from Notrios** verifies one without opening a database.

postcondition.narrative: the archive is written and the report says so

journeys.title: Take a snapshot of the library
journeys.goal: Write a verified snapshot image you can restore from.

steps.narrative: Open **File ▸ Import and export…**, or press Ctrl+I. Everything that reads or writes a folder on this machine is here, and it is here only in the desktop app: a browser cannot open a folder, so these controls are shown there and disabled with that reason rather than hidden.

locator.native: the File menu's “Import and export…” item

expect: the import and export dialog opened

steps.narrative: Name the folder to write the snapshot into. A snapshot is the whole library at one moment, and it is the fastest way to copy one that is going back into the same schema.

locator.native: the “Folder to write the snapshot into” field

steps.keys: Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab

steps.narrative: Press **Create snapshot**. The image is verified as it is written, and one that fails verification is never recorded as a snapshot. Restoring one is a command-line operation, because a restore replaces the library this window is showing.

postcondition.narrative: the snapshot is written and verified

journeys.title: Publish a subset of your notes
journeys.goal: Review exactly what a publication would let out, then write it.

steps.narrative: Open **File ▸ Import and export…**, or press Ctrl+I. Publishing is at the bottom, under the operations that read and write whole libraries, because it is the one that hands notes to somebody else.

locator.native: the File menu's “Import and export…” item

expect: the import and export dialog opened

steps.narrative: Choose a saved profile and press **Review what this would publish**. The counts lead with what is withheld and which links are rewritten, because that is the question — a publication carries current versions only, no trashed notes, no history and no provenance. Profiles are made with `notriosctl publish profile save` and only read here: a form that quietly defaulted a privacy choice is how something private gets published.

locator.native: the “Review what this would publish” button

steps.keys: Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Tab Return

steps.narrative: Name an empty folder — the caret is already in the field, because naming one is what the review just asked for — and press **Publish this review**. The run re-plans and refuses unless the plan still hashes to the one on screen, so what is published is what was read, not something rebuilt a moment later from the same profile.
The report names how many notes were written and where. A publication is not a backup: restoring from one is not a thing you can do, which is why the archive above exists.

postcondition.narrative: the publication is written and the report says how many notes went
